reports.label: CPO / Product Strategy — Market Fragmentation & Service Opportunity
reports.title: Market Insight: The Preemptive Cybersecurity Market Is Dangerously Fragmented — Full-Spectrum Vendors Will Define the Next Era
reports.summary: The preemptive cybersecurity market is defined by narrow specialization and capability silos. Of 51 vendors assessed across five capability pillars, only 27% demonstrate competency across the full spectrum. The vast majority of vendors — platform providers and service operators alike — compete in no more than three pillars, leaving buyers to assemble multi-vendor stacks to achieve comprehensive preemptive coverage. This fragmentation creates a strategic opportunity for vendors and MSSPs willing to build or acquire across the full spectrum of preemptive capabilities and deliver them as integrated outcomes.
reports.spa: By 2030, 30% of enterprise preemptive cybersecurity programs will be delivered through integrated platform-plus-service models spanning at least four of the five preemptive pillars, up from less than 5% today. Vendors that develop full-spectrum capability strategies — either through organic investment, acquisition, or managed service partnerships — by 2028 will capture disproportionate market share as buyers consolidate from fragmented multi-vendor environments to integrated preemptive platforms with service delivery.

findings.header: The preemptive cybersecurity market is fundamentally fragmented, with most vendors concentrating in three or fewer capability domains.
findings.body: Across the 51 vendors evaluated against five preemptive cybersecurity pillars — Exposure Management (EXM), Adversary Management & Threat Intelligence (AMT), Autonomous Detection & Response (ADR), Posture & Policy Management (PPM), and Services & Capabilities (SVC) — only 14 vendors (27%) demonstrate meaningful competency (score of 2.0 or higher) across all five pillars. Eighteen vendors (35%) are limited to three or fewer pillars. The average vendor covers 3.7 pillars, but this average masks significant concentration: vendors cluster heavily around EXM and PPM while neglecting adversary management and service delivery.

findings.header: Exposure Management and Posture Management dominate the market, while Adversary Management and Services represent critical blind spots.
findings.body: Pillar penetration rates reveal a lopsided market. Exposure Management (EXM) is addressed by 92% of vendors, and Posture & Policy Management (PPM) by 86%. In contrast, Adversary Management & Threat Intelligence (AMT) reaches only 55% of vendors, and Services & Capabilities (SVC) reaches only 57%. This means nearly half the market has no credible adversary intelligence capability and no service delivery model beyond basic implementation support. Buyers looking for integrated preemptive programs that include adversary-centric threat anticipation and managed delivery must navigate a fragmented vendor landscape with limited choices.

findings.header: Platform-only vendors have a structural service delivery deficit that limits their market ceiling.
findings.body: Twenty-five of 51 vendors (49%) operate as platform-only technology providers with no meaningful service delivery capability. These vendors average just 1.49 out of 5.0 on the Services & Capabilities pillar, with 88% scoring below the 2.0 competency threshold. Their strengths in technology — averaging 3.07 on EXM and 2.84 on PPM — are not complemented by any direct or partner-delivered managed service offering. As the market shifts toward outcome-based delivery, platform-only vendors without a service strategy will be confined to a shrinking addressable market of buyers willing and able to self-operate complex preemptive security tooling.

findings.header: Direct service providers have strong operational delivery but lack the platform depth of technology vendors.
findings.body: The 11 direct service providers — vendors that operate their own SOCs and analyst teams to deliver managed outcomes — score highest on SVC (averaging 2.74) and ADR (3.38), reflecting strong detection and response delivery. However, their Adversary Management scores average only 2.45, and several have gaps in Posture & Policy Management. The service delivery model is strong but narrow. These vendors deliver effective managed detection and response but rarely extend to proactive exposure management, adversary anticipation, or policy governance — the very capabilities that define preemptive cybersecurity.

findings.header: Platform-plus-partner vendors achieve broader coverage but dilute service accountability.
findings.body: The 15 platform-plus-partner vendors — those that provide technology and rely on MSSP/channel partners for managed service delivery — show the broadest pillar coverage, with the highest average AMT score (2.74) and strong PPM (3.21). However, their SVC scores average only 2.32, reflecting the inherent limitations of partner-delegated service delivery. The vendor builds the platform; the partner delivers the outcome. This model creates accountability gaps: when a managed service fails, the buyer is caught between the platform vendor and the service partner, with neither fully owning the outcome.

findings.header: Only three vendors achieve a minimum pillar score above 2.5 across all five domains — and they represent different delivery models.
findings.body: Mandiant (Google Cloud), SentinelOne, and Fortinet are the only vendors in the assessment with minimum pillar scores above 2.5 — meaning no significant blind spots across the full preemptive spectrum. Mandiant and SentinelOne are direct service providers; Fortinet is a platform-plus-partner model. The next tier (Rapid7, CrowdStrike, IBM Security) maintains min scores of 2.7+. This extreme concentration at the top illustrates how rare full-spectrum preemptive capability is today and how significant the differentiation opportunity is for vendors willing to invest across all five pillars.

recommendations.header: Map your current portfolio against the five preemptive pillars and identify structural gaps.
recommendations.body: Chief Product Officers should conduct an honest capability assessment of their current offerings against the five preemptive cybersecurity pillars: Exposure Management, Adversary Management & Threat Intelligence, Autonomous Detection & Response, Posture & Policy Management, and Services & Capabilities. Most vendors will find they are strong in two or three domains and structurally absent in others. This gap analysis should inform a multi-year product strategy that prioritizes the underrepresented pillars — particularly AMT and SVC, which are the market's most significant blind spots.

recommendations.header: Platform vendors must develop a credible service delivery strategy — organic, acquired, or partnered.
recommendations.body: The 49% of vendors operating as platform-only technology providers cannot compete in a market moving toward outcome-based delivery. Platform vendors should pursue one of three service strategies: (1) Build an internal managed service offering with a dedicated SOC and analyst team; (2) Acquire a managed service provider to gain delivery capability immediately; or (3) Formalize a structured partner delivery program with certified MSSPs, shared SLAs, and co-branded outcomes. The choice depends on scale, investment appetite, and time-to-market requirements — but the status quo of no service strategy is a strategic liability.

recommendations.header: Service providers should invest in platform depth and adversary intelligence to escape the MDR commodity trap.
recommendations.body: Direct service providers have strong operational delivery but risk being perceived as reactive managed security services. Investing in adversary management capabilities — threat anticipation, adversary profiling, attack surface intelligence — transforms the value proposition from 'we respond to what we detect' to 'we anticipate and prevent what would otherwise reach you.' The gap is real: even among direct service providers, 27% score below 2.0 on AMT. Filling this gap converts a managed service into a preemptive intelligence-driven program — a fundamentally different value proposition that commands premium pricing.

recommendations.header: Pursue strategic M&A to accelerate full-spectrum positioning rather than building every capability organically.
recommendations.body: With only 14 vendors achieving five-pillar coverage, the fastest path to full-spectrum positioning is acquisition. Platform vendors strong in EXM and PPM should target adversary intelligence specialists and managed service operators. Service providers with delivery strength should acquire exposure management or posture governance platforms. The fragmented market structure — with most vendors concentrated in one or two domains — creates a target-rich acquisition environment where niche specialists can be integrated to close specific pillar gaps within 12-18 months.

recommendations.header: Develop outcome-based commercial models that tie pricing to preemptive security results.
recommendations.body: Full-spectrum preemptive capability is only valuable if it can be commercially expressed as outcomes. Vendors achieving four or more pillar coverage should begin developing pricing models that go beyond seat-based or subscription licensing to include outcome-linked components: measurable reduction in exploitable exposure, attacker dwell-time commitments, proactive threat neutralization rates, and posture improvement benchmarks. This requires the measurement infrastructure that full-spectrum platforms provide — and it is the commercial translation of the strategic advantage that fragmented competitors cannot match.

recommendations.header: MSSPs should position as the integration layer that solves the fragmentation problem for buyers.
recommendations.body: The fragmented market creates a structural opportunity for managed security service providers to become the integration and orchestration layer. MSSPs can assemble multi-vendor preemptive stacks — combining best-of-breed EXM, AMT, ADR, and PPM platforms — and deliver them as a unified managed outcome. This positioning converts the market's fragmentation from a liability into a competitive advantage. MSSPs that develop deep integration playbooks across the five preemptive pillars and deliver them with SLA-backed outcomes will command premium margins and long-term contract commitments.

analysis_sections.title: The Five Pillars of Preemptive Cybersecurity and Why Full Coverage Matters
analysis_sections.body:
Preemptive cybersecurity represents a fundamental shift from reactive defense to proactive threat anticipation and neutralization. It encompasses five interconnected capability pillars, each addressing a distinct dimension of the preemptive posture:

- **Exposure Management (EXM)**: Continuous discovery, prioritization, and remediation of exploitable vulnerabilities and attack surface exposures before adversaries can exploit them. This is the market's strongest pillar, addressed by 92% of vendors.

- **Adversary Management & Threat Intelligence (AMT)**: Intelligence-driven understanding of adversary tactics, techniques, and infrastructure to anticipate attacks before they materialize. Only 55% of vendors address this pillar, making it the market's most significant gap after services.

- **Autonomous Detection & Response (ADR)**: AI-driven, automated detection and containment of threats with minimal human intervention, shifting from alert-based triage to autonomous threat neutralization. Addressed by 78% of vendors.

- **Posture & Policy Management (PPM)**: Continuous assessment and enforcement of security configuration, compliance, and policy alignment across the environment. Strong at 86% vendor coverage.

- **Services & Capabilities (SVC)**: The delivery layer — implementation, advisory, managed operations, and AI-driven service delivery that translates technology into outcomes. Only 57% of vendors demonstrate meaningful capability here.

The critical insight is that these pillars are interdependent. Exposure management without adversary intelligence prioritizes vulnerabilities by technical severity rather than adversary intent. Autonomous detection without posture governance responds to threats in misconfigured environments. Technology platforms without service delivery leave implementation and operational outcomes to the buyer. A preemptive cybersecurity program requires competency across all five pillars — and the market overwhelmingly fails to provide this.

analysis_sections.title: Market Fragmentation: By the Numbers
analysis_sections.body:
The fragmentation story is told by a single statistic: only 14 of 51 vendors (27%) achieve a score of 2.0 or higher across all five preemptive pillars. This means nearly three-quarters of the market has at least one structural blind spot.

The distribution reveals three distinct market segments:

**Full-spectrum vendors (14 vendors, 27%)**: These vendors score 2.0+ on all five pillars. They include both direct service providers (Mandiant, SentinelOne, CrowdStrike, Rapid7, Arctic Wolf, IBM Security, Fidelis Cybersecurity) and platform-plus-partner models (Tenable, Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, Lacework/Fortinet, Zscaler, Illumio, Akamai/Guardicore). Notably, no platform-only vendor achieves full-spectrum coverage, confirming that service delivery is the missing link.

**Majority-spectrum vendors (19 vendors, 37%)**: These vendors cover four pillars but have one significant gap. The most common missing pillar is SVC (Services) for platform-only vendors and AMT (Adversary Management) for others. These vendors are one strategic investment away from full-spectrum positioning.

**Narrow-spectrum vendors (18 vendors, 35%)**: These vendors cover three or fewer pillars. They include niche specialists (BAS platforms like AttackIQ, Pentera, SafeBreach), single-domain leaders (CyCognito in ASM, Recorded Future in threat intelligence), and vendors with incomplete market presence (Axonius, HashiCorp, Group-IB, Trellix — all scoring 0 on four of five pillars). These vendors compete on depth within their specialty but cannot address the integrated preemptive security use case.

analysis_sections.title: The Service Delivery Gap: Platform-Only Vendors and the Missing Link
analysis_sections.body:
The most strategically significant finding in this assessment is the structural service delivery gap among platform-only technology vendors. Twenty-five of 51 vendors (49%) — nearly half the market — have no meaningful service delivery capability.

These platform-only vendors average 1.49 on SVC, with individual sub-pillar scores revealing the depth of the gap:

- **SVC-01 (Implementation & Onboarding)**: Average scores around 2.0 — basic implementation support exists but is often limited to documentation and standard deployment guides.
- **SVC-02 (Consultative & Advisory)**: Moderate scores in the 2.0-2.5 range — most vendors offer some level of professional services or consulting engagement.
- **SVC-03 (Managed Operations)**: Scores capped at 1.0 for platform-only vendors — no managed service delivery option exists. This is by design: these vendors build tools, not services.
- **SVC-04 (AI-Driven Delivery)**: Scores capped at 1.0-1.5 — AI capabilities exist in the product but are not applied to service delivery because there is no service to deliver.

This creates a paradox: the most technologically sophisticated preemptive platforms cannot be translated into managed outcomes without a third-party service layer. Buyers must either self-operate complex tooling (requiring deep internal expertise) or engage a separate MSSP to operationalize the technology (adding cost, complexity, and accountability gaps).

For platform CPOs, this is both a risk and an opportunity. The risk is commoditization: as platforms converge on feature parity, the differentiator shifts from what the technology does to how it delivers outcomes. The opportunity is that the first platform vendors to crack the service delivery model — whether through internal build, acquisition, or structured partnerships — will establish a competitive moat that feature-level competitors cannot easily replicate.

analysis_sections.title: The Adversary Intelligence Deficit: Why Half the Market Flies Blind
analysis_sections.body:
Adversary Management & Threat Intelligence (AMT) is the second-largest capability gap in the market, with only 55% of vendors scoring 2.0 or higher. Among platform-only vendors, the gap is even more stark: 64% score below 2.0 on AMT.

This deficit has direct operational consequences. Without adversary intelligence, preemptive security degrades to reactive vulnerability management. Exposure prioritization is driven by CVSS scores and technical severity rather than adversary intent and exploitation probability. Detection rules are based on known indicators rather than predicted adversary behavior. Security posture is measured against compliance frameworks rather than real-world threat landscapes.

The vendors that combine strong AMT with other pillars — Aqua Security (3.8 AMT), Morphisec (3.9 AMT), CyberArk (3.6 AMT), BeyondTrust (3.6 AMT) — use adversary intelligence to sharpen every other capability. Their exposure management is informed by which vulnerabilities adversaries are actively targeting. Their detection models incorporate adversary TTP patterns. Their posture benchmarks reflect the actual threat environment.

For CPOs evaluating portfolio strategy, AMT is an underinvested domain with outsized impact. Building or acquiring adversary intelligence capability transforms every other pillar from reactive to anticipatory — and the market opportunity is large, with 45% of vendors currently unable to offer this differentiation.

analysis_sections.title: Three Delivery Models, Three Strategic Trade-Offs
analysis_sections.body:
The market splits into three distinct delivery models, each with structural strengths and limitations:

**Direct Service Providers (11 vendors, 22%)** — These vendors operate their own security operations centers, employ dedicated analyst teams, and deliver managed outcomes directly to clients. They are the most balanced segment, with the highest average SVC scores (2.74) and strong ADR capabilities (3.38). Their strategic advantage is operational accountability: when the service fails, there is one throat to choke. Their limitation is platform depth: average EXM (3.60) and PPM (2.97) scores trail behind platform vendors, reflecting an operational model optimized for service delivery rather than comprehensive platform capability.

**Platform-Plus-Partner Vendors (15 vendors, 29%)** — These vendors build technology platforms and rely on MSSP and channel partners for managed service delivery. They show the broadest pillar coverage overall, with the highest AMT (2.74) and PPM (3.21) averages, reflecting deep platform investment. Their limitation is the partner-mediated service model: SVC averages 2.32, and the quality of service delivery depends on partner capability, not vendor commitment. This introduces accountability gaps that become visible when managed services underperform.

**Platform-Only Vendors (25 vendors, 49%)** — Pure technology providers with no service delivery mechanism. They have the lowest scores on every pillar except none, with particularly weak AMT (1.87) and SVC (1.49). They compete on technology capability within their specialization but cannot address the integrated, managed preemptive security use case. Their strategic ceiling is defined by the buyer's ability and willingness to self-operate the platform.

The strategic takeaway: no single delivery model has solved the full-spectrum challenge. Direct service providers lack platform depth. Platform vendors lack service delivery. Partner models lack accountability. The vendor that integrates platform innovation with accountable service delivery across all five pillars will define the next era of preemptive cybersecurity.

analysis_sections.title: The Full-Spectrum Opportunity: What 2030 Looks Like
analysis_sections.body:
The current market fragmentation creates a window of strategic opportunity that will narrow as consolidation accelerates. By 2030, we project the following market evolution:

**Phase 1 — Platform Extension (2025-2026)**: Leading platform vendors begin acquiring or building adjacent pillar capabilities. EXM-strong vendors add AMT through threat intelligence acquisitions. ADR platforms extend into PPM through compliance automation. The driver is customer demand for fewer vendor relationships and integrated dashboards.

**Phase 2 — Service Layer Development (2026-2028)**: Platform vendors that achieved three or four pillar coverage begin developing managed service delivery models. This manifests as formal MSSP certification programs, white-label managed service offerings, or acquisitions of regional service providers. The 88% of platform-only vendors currently below 2.0 on SVC will shrink to below 50% by 2028.

**Phase 3 — Integrated Outcome Delivery (2028-2030)**: The convergence of full-spectrum platform capability with managed service delivery enables outcome-based commercial models. Vendors offer measurable preemptive security outcomes — quantified reduction in exploitable exposure, adversary dwell-time guarantees, autonomous remediation rates — tied to commercial terms. This is the strategic endgame, and it requires competency across all five pillars to credibly deliver.

**Market impact projections**:
- The number of vendors achieving five-pillar coverage will grow from 14 (27%) to over 25 (50%+) through organic investment and M&A
- At least 5 major platform vendors will launch branded managed preemptive security services
- The addressable market for integrated preemptive programs (spanning 4+ pillars with managed delivery) will exceed $8 billion, growing at more than double the rate of point-product cybersecurity markets
- MSSPs that develop preemptive specialization across 4+ pillars will command 30-40% pricing premiums over generalist managed security providers

The vendors that begin this strategic journey now — in 2025 and 2026 — will have a 3-5 year head start that late movers cannot easily close. Full-spectrum preemptive security requires deep integration across pillars, operational maturity in service delivery, and commercial innovation in outcome-based pricing. These are not capabilities that can be acquired overnight.

reports.background:
The preemptive cybersecurity market represents an emerging category that shifts the security paradigm from reactive detection and response to proactive threat anticipation and neutralization. Unlike traditional cybersecurity approaches that focus on identifying and containing threats after they penetrate defenses, preemptive cybersecurity aims to eliminate exploitable conditions, anticipate adversary behavior, and neutralize attack paths before breaches occur.

This assessment evaluated 51 vendors across five capability pillars — Exposure Management (EXM), Adversary Management & Threat Intelligence (AMT), Autonomous Detection & Response (ADR), Posture & Policy Management (PPM), and Services & Capabilities (SVC) — each scored on a 1-5 maturity scale with defined sub-pillar criteria. Vendors were additionally classified by delivery model: direct service providers (11 vendors) that operate their own SOCs and deliver managed outcomes, platform-plus-partner models (15 vendors) that build technology and rely on channel/MSSP partners for service delivery, and platform-only providers (25 vendors) that offer technology licensing with no managed service component.

The overall market reveals strong but uneven capability maturity. Exposure Management leads with 92% vendor coverage and the highest average scores, reflecting the market's origins in vulnerability management and attack surface discovery. Posture & Policy Management follows at 86%, driven by compliance automation and configuration governance demand. However, Adversary Management (55% coverage) and Services & Capabilities (57% coverage) represent significant market gaps that constrain the effectiveness of preemptive programs.

The vendor population spans the full spectrum of cybersecurity market participants — from hyperscale platform vendors (CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet) to niche specialists (Pentera, AttackIQ, CyCognito) to managed service operators (Arctic Wolf, Mandiant). This diversity makes the fragmentation findings more significant: the gap is not between large and small vendors but between the very few that have assembled comprehensive preemptive capability and the many that remain locked into one or two specializations.
reports.impact:
The implications of market fragmentation differ significantly by audience, but the common thread is urgency: the window for strategic positioning is open now and will narrow as consolidation reshapes the competitive landscape.

**For Platform / Technology Vendors (CPO Perspective)**:
The core strategic question is whether to remain a point-product vendor competing on feature depth within one or two pillars, or to invest in becoming a preemptive platform that spans four or more pillars with integrated service delivery. The data makes the case for breadth: the 14 full-spectrum vendors average 3.35 across all pillars, while three-pillar vendors average 2.67 — a gap that reflects both broader capability and deeper specialization within each domain. Full-spectrum vendors are not sacrificing depth for breadth; they are achieving both.

The service delivery imperative is even more pressing. Platform-only vendors average 1.49 on SVC compared to 2.74 for direct service providers. This is not a minor gap — it represents a fundamentally different market position. As buyers increasingly demand managed outcomes rather than self-operated tools, platform-only vendors without a service strategy face addressable market contraction.

**For Managed Service Providers (MSSP/MDR CPO Perspective)**:
The fragmented technology landscape is an advantage if service providers can become the integration and orchestration layer. Today, MSSPs typically specialize in detection and response — essentially the ADR pillar. By developing expertise across exposure management, adversary intelligence, and posture governance, MSSPs can offer integrated preemptive programs that no individual platform vendor can match. This positioning justifies premium pricing and longer contract terms.

The risk for MSSPs is remaining reactive. The market's largest service delivery gaps are in proactive capabilities: adversary anticipation, exposure prioritization, and posture enforcement. MSSPs that extend from reactive MDR into proactive preemptive operations will differentiate sharply from the growing field of commodity managed detection providers.

**For the Broader Market**:
The fragmentation creates short-term buying complexity and long-term consolidation pressure. Enterprise buyers assembling preemptive security programs today must integrate three to five vendors across different pillars, manage separate contracts and SLAs, and accept accountability gaps between technology and service providers. This complexity tax is substantial, and it creates strong buyer pull for vendors that can reduce it through integrated offerings.

Consolidation will accelerate as full-spectrum positioning becomes table stakes. We expect the current ratio of 14 full-spectrum vendors (27% of market) to grow to 50%+ by 2030, driven by M&A activity focused on filling pillar gaps — particularly AMT and SVC acquisitions by platform-strong vendors.
reports.conclusion:
The preemptive cybersecurity market is at an inflection point defined by a central paradox: the security approach that buyers need — proactive, multi-pillar, outcome-oriented — is one that almost no vendor currently delivers comprehensively. Only 27% of vendors cover all five preemptive pillars, and only three achieve a minimum score above 2.5 across the full spectrum.

This fragmentation is not a market failure — it is a market opportunity. The vendors that move now to build full-spectrum capability, develop credible service delivery models, and create outcome-based commercial structures will establish competitive positions that narrow-spectrum competitors cannot easily challenge.

The path forward differs by starting position. Platform vendors should prioritize adversary intelligence and service delivery — the two largest market gaps. Service providers should invest in platform depth and proactive capability to escape the reactive MDR commodity trap. MSSPs should position as the orchestration layer that solves the multi-vendor integration problem buyers face today.

For Chief Product Officers, three strategic questions should drive investment decisions:

1. **How many of the five preemptive pillars does our portfolio credibly address today?** If the answer is three or fewer, pillar expansion should be a strategic priority. If four, service delivery is likely the missing piece.

2. **Can we deliver preemptive outcomes, or do we deliver tools that require the buyer to create outcomes?** The distinction between technology vendors and outcome vendors will define competitive positioning by 2028.

3. **Do we have a path to full-spectrum coverage by 2028?** Whether through organic investment, acquisition, or structured partnerships, the window to establish preemptive market position is two to three years. Vendors that reach full-spectrum first will set the competitive standard that followers must match.

The preemptive cybersecurity market will consolidate around vendors that can credibly answer 'yes' to all three questions. Start now.

glossary.definition: Exposure Management. Continuous discovery, prioritization, and remediation of exploitable vulnerabilities and attack surface exposures.
Adversary Management & Threat Intelligence. Intelligence-driven understanding of adversary tactics, techniques, and infrastructure to anticipate attacks.
Autonomous Detection & Response. AI-driven, automated detection and containment of threats with minimal human intervention.
Posture & Policy Management. Continuous assessment and enforcement of security configuration, compliance, and policy alignment.
Services & Capabilities. The delivery layer encompassing implementation, advisory, managed operations, and AI-driven service delivery.
A security paradigm focused on proactively anticipating and neutralizing threats before they materialize, rather than reacting to incidents after they occur.
Vendor capability across all five preemptive pillars (EXM, AMT, ADR, PPM, SVC) at a competency threshold of 2.0 or higher on a 5-point scale.
A vendor that operates its own security operations center and analyst team to deliver managed security outcomes directly to clients.
A vendor delivery model where the vendor builds the technology platform and relies on MSSP or channel partners for managed service delivery.
A vendor that offers technology licensing with no managed service delivery option, requiring buyers to self-operate or engage third-party service providers.
Managed Security Service Provider. A third-party organization that delivers managed security operations, monitoring, and response services using vendor technology platforms.
Breach and Attack Simulation. Technology that validates security controls by simulating real-world attack techniques in production environments.
Attack Surface Management. Continuous discovery and monitoring of an organization's external-facing digital assets and exposures.
Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures. The behavioral patterns and methods used by cyber adversaries, as cataloged in frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK.
Cyber Asset Attack Surface Management. Technology that aggregates and correlates asset data across tools to provide comprehensive visibility.
Automated Moving Target Defense. Technology that continuously changes the attack surface to make exploitation unpredictable and costly for adversaries.

evidence: Gartner Preemptive Cybersecurity Vendor Assessment, 2025-2026 — 51-vendor evaluation across 5 capability pillars and 24 sub-pillar dimensions.
Vendor delivery model classification based on public documentation, service pages, partner program structures, and MSSP partner locator analysis.
Pillar coverage analysis: 14/51 vendors (27%) achieve 5-pillar coverage >= 2.0; 33/51 (65%) achieve 4+ pillar coverage.
Pillar penetration rates: EXM 92%, PPM 86%, ADR 78%, SVC 57%, AMT 55%.
Platform-only SVC deficit: 88% of 25 platform-only vendors score below 2.0 on Services & Capabilities.
Top-3 most balanced vendors by minimum pillar score: Mandiant (min 2.8), SentinelOne (min 2.8), Fortinet (min 2.8).

Average pillar scores by delivery model — Direct Service: EXM 3.60, AMT 2.45, ADR 3.38, PPM 2.97, SVC 2.74; Platform+Partner: EXM 3.69, AMT 2.74, ADR 2.83, PPM 3.21, SVC 2.32; Platform-Only: EXM 3.07, AMT 1.87, ADR 2.52, PPM 2.84, SVC 1.49.
